articles.title: U.S. Open 2026: How to watch, full TV schedule, streaming info and more
articles.summary: This weekend, the singles tournament kicks off at the 2026 U.S. Open. Here's how to tune in.
articles.body:
The 2026 U.S. Open tennis tournament begins in earnest this Sunday, Aug. 30. This year will see some big names on the court, including Aryna Sabalenka, Elena Rybakina, Jessica Pegula, Coco Gauff, Carlos Alcaraz, Novak Djokovic, Ben Shelton, Taylor Fritz and Serena and Venus Williams, competing in doubles as a wild card entry .

The tournament will air across ESPN, ESPN2 and ABC. You can stream every match with an ESPN Unlimited subscription. Disney+ subscribers can catch all the Day 1 action in-app, no add-on required.

Here's everything you need to know to watch the 2026 U.S. Open tennis tournament, including the full TV schedule, where to stream matches without cable and more.

TV channel: ESPN, ESPN2, ABC, ESPN Deportes

The U.S. Open singles tournament kicks off on Sunday, Aug. 30, and concludes with the Men's Championship on Sunday, Sept. 13.

The ESPN suite will cover the entirety of the 2026 U.S. Open, with daily coverage of all 16 courts airing across ESPN, ESPN2, ESPN Deportes (Spanish) and streaming on the ESPN App for ESPN Unlimited plan subscribers.

ABC will broadcast all three Sundays of the tournament, including first round coverage, Round of 16 matches and the Men's Championship Preview and Championship.

ESPN Unlimited subscribers will be ale to stream the entirety of the U.S. Open, plus, all Disney+ subscribers can access select Day 1 action directly within the app, even without a bundle subscription to ESPN.

articles.title: Roger Federer Inducted into Hall of Fame, Top Photos, Videos and Quotes from Tennis Icon's Speech
articles.summary: Roger Federer was officially inducted into the International Tennis Hall of Fame in Newport, Rhode Island on Saturday.
articles.body:
Roger Federer was officially inducted into the International Tennis Hall of Fame in Newport, Rhode Island on Saturday.

Federer was recognized for his legendary career with a ceremony on the historic Horseshoe Court.

Gauff's mom calls out family, friends asking for tickets

His wife, Mirka, introduced him at the event.

He followed it up with an emotional speech in which he detailed his journey from childhood to his professional tennis career and thanked the friends, family and fellow players that helped him along the way.

"This boy from Basel thanks you for the incredible honor and I thank all of you for sharing the journey that brought us together," Federer said (27:47 mark).

Federer also received video messages from friends and rivals including Novak Djokovic and Grigor Dimitrov as they congratulated him on his Hall of Fame induction.

Federer retired from tennis professionally in 2022, ending a stellar career in which he racked up 103 ATP Tour singles titles and 20 Grand Slam championships. He captured two Olympic medals as well.

Federer also spent 237 weeks at No. 1 in the ATP rankings from 2004-08, representing the longest streak of all time.

Now, his tennis legacy is reflected in the Hall of Fame.

articles.title: Carlos Alcaraz returns to US Open after four-month injury layoff with tennis world watching
articles.summary: Tennis News: New York City: Four months is a long time in tennis.Since Carlos Alcaraz injured his right wrist in a fateful moment in mid-April, the men’s tour, lik.
articles.body: New York City: Four months is a long time in tennis.Since Carlos Alcaraz injured his right wrist in a fateful moment in mid-April, the men’s tour, like the swirling seasons, has changed.Alexander Zverev won his first Grand Slam title at 29 during a fortnight when temperatures soared at Roland Garros, while world No. 1 Jannik Sinner defended his Wimbledon title. Spanish teenager Rafael Jodar shot up the ATP rankings, climbing from outside the top 500 to the brink of the world’s top 10 in less than a year.It is into this unpredictable landscape that a new-look Alcaraz walks in. The 23-year-old, however, will take comfort from the fact that he returns to competitive tennis at the US Open, the Grand Slam where it all began for him.It was at this sprawling venue in New York’s Queens borough in 2022 that he claimed his maiden major crown and climbed to No. 1 in the rankings for the first time. It was here that he returned to the pinnacle again last year, defeating Sinner to claim his second US Open title.On Monday, Alcaraz, whose long, flowy locks, held back by a thin black headband, have already attracted plenty of wows from the fandom, opens against Roman Safiullin, the 29-year-old who lit up Wimbledon with his fight last month. The Russian also defeated Alcaraz in straight sets at the Paris Masters three years ago.The two most recent Masters 1000 champions, Ben Shelton and Arthur Fils, are potential quarterfinal opponents for second-seeded Alcaraz, who has 24-time major winner Novak Djokovic in his half.“I’m feeling great,” Alcaraz told international media at his pre-championship conference. “I think that right now it’s (injury) all in my head. I gotta trust my team, I gotta trust my people that tell me it’s gonna be fine. So I just have to go 100%, and stay away from that fear.”“My team and I believe that I’m ready,” he added. “It wasn’t an easy decision. I did whatever it took to be ready. I tried to do everything perfect on and off the court, really long practices, intense practices, just to see how my wrist is going to react.”Alcaraz practised with the 23-year-old Holger Rune, the big-hitting former No. 4, in Murcia before arriving in New York.Even though Alcaraz enters the US Open after a four-month injury break and without a prior hard-court singles match, the second seed is hardly short of expectations. If anything, the last few months have underlined just how much Alcaraz, Sinner and the 39-year-old Djokovic matter to the men’s game.They are the sport’s biggest stars, the ones who put bums on seats. At Roland Garros in May-June, with Alcaraz out of tournament play and Sinner’s challenge wilting in the heat, Zverev’s title run became an uncomfortable one for the sport. The German’s two separate sets of domestic abuse allegations reshaped the way he has been covered in parts of the media.Now, with Sinner out with a dodgy right knee, the onus to carry the load for his generation falls on Alcaraz.Daniil Medvedev, the 30-year-old world No. 8, argued that if Alcaraz is at Flushing Meadows, it means he and his team are confident that the wrist has sufficiently recovered.“I don’t think the wrist is going to be a problem,” he said. “It’s more for the whole body itself. If he has a tough match, it could be interesting to see how he copes. It’s really nice for me to see him here to play. If I have a chance, I’m going to watch his match, he’s playing my friend Roman.”Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: US Open 2026 singles preview: Will Aryna Sabalenka rediscover her mojo? How will Carlos Alcaraz fare on comeback?
articles.summary: Will Aryna Sabalenka rediscover her mojo? How will Carlos Alcaraz's comeback go? And can Novak Djokovic win? It's time for the 2026 US Open singles.
articles.body:
All was bright in Aryna Sabalenka's world when she completed a rare 'Sunshine Double' earlier this season.

Becoming only the fifth woman to win the Indian Wells and Miami titles back-to-back, Sabalenka emphasised her position as the dominant player on the WTA Tour and created a 3,000-point lead at the top of the world rankings.

But a difficult period quickly followed - seemingly out of nowhere - leaving the 28-year-old Belarusian clinging on to her position going into the US Open, which starts on Sunday.

Two-time defending champion Sabalenka returns to New York with a 17-7 win-loss record since the Miami triumph, including a chastening French Open quarter-final exit and a disheartening defeat in the Wimbledon fourth round.

It is a record far below the four-time major winner's lofty standards.

With 2,000 points to defend at Flushing Meadows and Kazakhstan's Elena Rybakina now trailing by only 434, Sabalenka must win again to extend her 99-week run as the world number one.

Asked if she felt confident she can rediscover her mojo on the hard courts on which she has thrived, Sabalenka said: "Absolutely. These tough lessons are definitely going to make me way, way stronger and working even harder."

Tough US Open draw for Alcaraz - who else plays who?

'A generational icon' - why wildcards abound for Venus Williams

Sabalenka's four Grand Slam singles titles - two Australian Open and two US Open triumphs, all on hard courts - are more than most players can dream of.

However, she has also lost four major finals and six semi-finals, despite a consistency on the biggest stages that is unrivalled among her peers.

The concern in recent months has been Sabalenka's mental focus disappearing in less pressurised situations.

This was most recently apparent in her Cincinnati Open fourth-round defeat by 20-year-old Czech opponent Sara Bejlek. Sabalenka led 5-1 in a first-set tie-break and 4-1 in the second set, but continued to lack composure in the rallies as Bejlek rallied to win 7-6 (9-7) 6-4.

At her previous tournament in Toronto, she lost to Russian world number 19 Ekaterina Alexandrova in the last 16 as her serve crumbled.

During the clay-court swing, Sabalenka capitulated after winning the first set against Hailey Baptiste in Madrid, Sorana Cirstea in Rome and, most notably, Diana Shnaider at Roland Garros.

"I work on my mental side of the game. I've been trying to reset my mind and to come back stronger," a bullish Sabalenka said in New York.

"It's only a matter of time for me to come back."

The drop-off in Sabalenka's results have opened the door for Rybakina, who beat the Belarusian to win the Australian Open in January, to take over as world number one.

Rybakina might not even have to win a match at Flushing Meadows to do that, as she has fewer ranking points to defend than Sabalenka.

However, there are questions over her fitness because of an ankle injury sustained in the Cincinnati quarter-finals.

Rybakina can secure the number one ranking if her nearest rivals - Sabalenka, Jessica Pegula and Coco Gauff - do not win the title.

If Sabalenka does retain the title, Rybakina would still also rise to the top by reaching the semi-finals.

Pegula, 32, has been ultra-consistent for several seasons without landing a major title, but the 2024 finalist hopes her runs to the Washington and Cincinnati finals will provide the platform for another crack at her home Slam.

Gauff, who beat Pegula to the Cincinnati trophy last week, already has the experience of winning in New York after claiming her first major there in 2023.

Twelve months ago, the 22-year-old American's game was clouded by uncertainty but returns with more confidence and fluidity in her serve.

Beneath the leading quartet, the rest of the top 10 also hold either a Grand Slam or WTA 1,000 title - a group led by French Open winner Mirra Andreeva, Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova and six-time major winner Iga Swiatek.

"You can just see how the depth is pretty crazy," said Pegula.

Williams sisters given US Open doubles wildcard

Newlywed Boulter won't repeat Murray's ring mistake

Will someone take advantage of 'Sincaraz' injury issues?

For the third Grand Slam in a row, the rivalry between Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz has been put on hold.

The pair swept all eight major titles between them in 2024 and 2025, with Alcaraz extending that run with victory at this year's Australian Open.

But the pair have not competed at the same Grand Slam since.

Alcaraz missed the French Open and Wimbledon with a wrist injury, and makes his comeback from a four-month absence in New York.

A day after the 23-year-old Spaniard announced his plan to return, Sinner revealed he had been ruled out with a knee issue.

"It's kind of weird. We are not going see each other for, like, six months now, seven months," said Alcaraz.

Sinner's absence and the uncertainty around Alcaraz's fitness will galvanise the rest of the chasing pack - particularly 39-year-old Novak Djokovic.

The Serb great, a 24-time Grand Slam champion, insists he has not put an "expiry date" on his extraordinary career. He continues to put himself in the mix for titles as he looks to finally land a standalone record 25th victory which would move him clear of Australia's Margaret Court on the all-time list.

He has reached at least the semi-finals in six of the past seven Slams, but has not gone all the way since triumphing at the 2023 US Open.

Germany's Alexander Zverev leads the seedings as he looks to reach a third straight major final, having won his first Slam at the French Open before losing to Sinner at Wimbledon.

Canadian Open champion Ben Shelton and Cincinnati finalist Frances Tiafoe lead a strong American challenge, while 2024 finalist Taylor Fritz is another hope capable of ending a 23-year wait for a home men's champion.

articles.title: ‘Oh gosh, this such a mess’: Roger Federer breaks down during Hall of Fame speech - Watch
articles.summary: Tennis News: Roger Federer became emotional several times during his induction speech at the International Tennis Hall of Fame in Newport on Saturday, reflecting o.
articles.body: Roger Federer became emotional several times during his induction speech at the International Tennis Hall of Fame in Newport on Saturday, reflecting on his career, family and the people who helped him along the way.The 45-year-old Swiss great, who won 20 Grand Slam singles titles, was inducted alongside former player and broadcaster Mary Carillo.Federer was introduced by his wife, Mirka, and admitted that following her speech would be difficult.“Oh man,” were the first words from the first man ever to win 20 Grand Slam singles titles. “This is very high level and a tough act to follow.”He later joked: “I don't know if you have been practicing secretly” before praising Mirka.During his nearly 30-minute speech, Federer became emotional while remembering childhood hero Stefan Edberg, longtime coach Severin Luthi and, most importantly, Mirka.Watch:“Now the Mirka part,” he said, pausing before breaking into tears. “Oh gosh, this such a mess.”As he tried to regain his composure, Federer told the audience, “I need tissues and sunglasses, everything to protect me right now.”A career filled with historic achievementsFederer finished his speech by thanking the ball boys and encouraging future players to continue pushing tennis forward. His remarkable career included eight Wimbledon titles, six Australian Opens and one French Open, making him one of only eight men to complete a career Grand Slam.“I'm thrilled to have made the journey here,” he said. “It's amazing to see yourself in a place like this. To immerse yourself in the history of the sport means a lot to me.”Carillo, inducted as a contributor, was also deeply moved by the honour.King said: “She has earned her spot in sports journalism and she has earned her spot in Newport.”Carillo added: “To walk through these gates here in the company of you people, that was beyond my dreams.”Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Alcaraz regresa en el US Open con el espejo de Nadal y Federer: "Ellos demostraron que se puede ganar"
articles.standfirst: El murciano no se descarta en la lucha por el último grande de la temporada
articles.summary: El murciano no se descarta en la lucha por el último grande de la temporada
articles.body: Las estadísticas están para romperse y a eso se agarra Carlos Alcaraz, el número 1 más precoz de la historia y el más joven en reinar en los cuatro grandes escenarios de la raqueta y completar así el Grand Slam. Alcaraz, que se rodó el martes en el mixto del US Open al lado de Serena Williams, debuta este lunes en la competición individual ante el ruso Roman Safiullin (19.30 horas). Habrán pasado 139 días desde la lesión que se produjo en su muñeca derecha en la ronda inicial del Barcelona Open Banc Sabadell. Después de muchas dudas, sobre todo tras borrarse de Cincinnati, el murciano está sano para afrontar lo que resta de temporada. Desde Roger Federer, en 2008, nadie ha sido capaz de defender el cetro de campeón del Abierto de los Estados Unidos. Y ningún tenista fue capaz de levantar el trofeo del último major del curso sin un rodaje previo desde la introducción de los Masters 1000 en 1990. “Odio perder. Yo vengo a por todas, pero para mí lo más importante es salir de este torneo sano, haber podido competir, entrenarme con grandes jugadores, que me hayan respetado la muñeca y el resto del cuerpo. No sé si mi tope va a ser la primera ronda, la segunda o llegar a la final. No quiero pensar en el resultado, sino en el proceso, en todo lo que estamos haciendo y, sobre todo, en salir ahí, disfrutar y sentirme bien, que es algo que llevo mucho tiempo queriendo sentir en una pista de tenis”, reflexiona. El tenista de El Palmar, conocedor de la historia del tenis, sabe que Federer y Rafael Nadal grandes títulos después de una larga inactividad. Roger sumó su penúltimo Grand Slam, en Wimbledon 2017, después de ausentarse del circuito desde Miami. Nadal, por su parte, se impuso en el Open de Australia 2022 tras permanecer seis meses parado. “Como poder, se puede. Creo que mucha gente lo ha demostrado. Es el caso de Federer, Rafa…, que demostraron que se puede ganar un Grand Slam después de haber estado lesionado mucho tiempo o de haber tenido una lesión muy dura, así que vamos a intentar agarrarnos a la idea de que también se puede”, dice el segundo favorito del cuadro. Alcaraz es el principal reclamo de un torneo neoyorquino que contará con la sensible baja de Jannik Sinner por la rodilla y la vuelta de Serena para juntarse en dobles con su hermana Venus. Para la ocasión, el pupilo de Samuel López lucirá una equipación sin mangas Nike inspirada en el habitual conjunto de los Knicks de Nueva York, flamantes campeones de la NBA en 2026. “Creo que no hay mejor torneo que el US Open para volver y sentir el cariño y la cálida bienvenida”, avisa. La ciudad de los rascacielos se ilumina con Carlitos.

articles.title: Sabalenka pone el número 1 WTA a subasta en Nueva York
articles.standfirst: Rybakina, que depende de ella, Pegula y Gauff aspiran a destronar a la bielorrusa de lo más alto
articles.summary: Rybakina, que depende de ella, Pegula y Gauff aspiran a destronar a la bielorrusa de lo más alto
articles.body: Tres tenistas, Elena Rybakina, Jessica Pegula y Coco Gauff, quieren pescar en el actual desgobierno de la WTA. La dominación de Aryna Sabalenka e Iga Swiatek se acabó y Rybakina, Pegula y Gauff optan a arrebatarle a Sabalenka el número uno mundial. Esta lo retiene desde el 21 de octubre de 2024. La regularidad de la bielorrusa tocó precisamente a su fin en el US Open 2025. Desde entonces, falló en el Open de Australia (finalista), Roland Garros (cuartofinalista) y Wimbledon (octavofinalista). Sus resultados han ido decreciendo, pero en Nueva York se convertirá en la sexta jugadora con más tiempo de permanencia en lo más alto, con un total de 99 semanas. Desde Serena Williams (2012-14) ninguna profesional ha sido capaz de ganar tres veces consecutivas en las pistas de Flushing Meadows. Las estadísticas juegan en contra de Sabakenka porque los últimos siete majors han ido a parar a rostros distintos. El récord sin que nadie repita son ocho. La kazaja, que se vio obligada a retirarse por el tendón de Aquiles en los cuartos de Cincinnati, será la nueva líder de la WTA si se mete en las semifinales con independencia de lo que hagan las demás. Elena se encuentra en algodones y ni tan siquiera ha asegurado su presencia en la primera ronda con la desconocida Thea Frodin, la 580 del mundo. Las opciones de Sabalenka, Pegula y Gauff pasan por ganar el título. A diferencia de Wimbledon, donde aceptó una invitación para el cuadro individual, Serena Williams ha optado por jugar el mixto con Carlos Alcaraz y el dobles junto a su hermanísima Venus. La pequeña de la familia, que el 26 de septiembre cumplirá 45 años, se despidió oficialmente del tenis hace cuatro temporadas. Fue tras perder en la tercera ronda del Abierto de los Estados Unidos con Ajla Tomljanovic. La Armada femenina acude sin grandes expectativas. El rendimiento de Paula Badosa es una incógnita tras la intervención a la que se sometió la catalana y que la ha dejado sin competir desde el pasado mes de julio.

articles.title: Dani Mérida, un tenista con reloj: "Es ligero y no lo noto al jugar"
articles.standfirst: El madrileño tiene como uno de sus patrocinadores a la marca de relojes de lujo Gerald Charles
articles.summary: El madrileño tiene como uno de sus patrocinadores a la marca de relojes de lujo Gerald Charles
articles.body: Los buenos resultados de Dani Mérida, el 39 del ranking a sus 21 años, no han pasado inadvertidos para las grandes marcas. El madrileño es una de las revelaciones de la presente temporada y ha aprovechado su estancia en Nueva York, con motivo del US Open, para asistir a la presentación de los relojes de lujo Gerald Charles. Su precio va desde los 17.000 euros a los 60.000. La marca suiza ha apostado por Mérida, que juega con uno de ellos desde el pasado Masters 1000 de Roma. Fue antes, en el Mutua Madrid Open, cuando se rezó el acuerdo entre los representantes de Gerald Charles y David Tosas, agente de Dani en 'The Agency'. "Estoy muy contento de jugar con reloj porque es ligero y no molesta. Para nada me supone un punto negativo en la pista porque no lo noto jugando", cuenta el flamante campeón de Umag. Fue en tierras croatas donde estrenó su palmarés de títulos el pasado mes de julio. Dani, que debuta este domingo en el último grande contra el húngaro Marton Fucsovics, está fichado por Dunlop (raquetas), Asics (ropa y calzado hasta final de curso) y también presta su imagen a Revel, una compañía de renting de coches. Se hizo familiar su rostro en los descansos de Wimbledon con un anuncio que se veía por televisión. Nueva York está pendiente del joven valor de la 'Armada'.

articles.title: El último tren de Djokovic en Nueva York: "Siento que estoy preparado"
articles.standfirst: El serbio reconoce que le fue bien perder pronto en el Masters 1000 de Cincinnati
articles.summary: El serbio reconoce que le fue bien perder pronto en el Masters 1000 de Cincinnati
articles.body: Novak Djokovic aparece por vigésima ocasión en el cuadro final del US Open, algo que sólo habían logrado antes tres jugadores. A sus 39 años, el serbio sigue buscando el título de Grand Slam que le deje solo en lo más alto del palmarés de los 'majors'. En la actualidad empata a 24 con la australiana Margaret Court. Su travesía por el desierto se alarga tres temporadas. Y es que para encontrar su último gran éxito hay que remontarse al Abierto de los Estados Unidos 2023 cuando derrotó en la final al ruso Daniil Medvedev. "Estoy muy orgulloso de llegar a 20 presencias en Nueva York. Obviamente, la longevidad siempre fue una de mis metas cuando era más joven: Intentar tener una carrera larga, buscar más oportunidades en los Grand Slams y mantenerme sano el tiempo suficiente para poder competir durante la mayor cantidad de años posible", reflexiona. Djokovic se refirió a sus compañeros de viaje durante todo ese tiempo, con los que coincide estos días en las pistas de Flushing Meadows: "He visto por ahí que somos unos tres o cuatro los que jugábamos ya en 2006, creo. Me parece que eran Wawrinka, quizás Monfils, y Cilic. Así que es agradable, en cierto modo, retroceder en el tiempo". El tenista de Belgrado, que la pasada campaña fue directo a Nueva York sin un rodaje previo, reconoce que le fue bien la pronta derrota en el reciente Masters 1000 de Cincinnati con el argentino Tirante. Cabe recodar que en Ohio sufrió con el calor y la humedad, unos elementos que también se va a encontrar en el último grande del curso. "La verdad es que no me gusta perder en las primeras rondas de ningún torneo, pero eso me dio tiempo para prepararme para el US Open de la mejor manera posible. Tuve varias semanas para entrenar de verdad y poner mi cuerpo y mi mente en el estado adecuado, listo para lo que se avecina. Si me preguntas si estoy preparado, siento que sí; estoy lo mejor que puedo estar, pero una cosa es entrenar y otra muy distinta salir a la pista del estadio Arthur Ashe y jugar partidos al mejor de cinco sets", se sincera.

articles.title: US Open: Aryna Sabalenka’s New York test is about more than No. 1
articles.summary: Tennis News: NEW YORK CITY: Aryna Sabalenka arrived at Flushing Meadows chasing history. She could leave it without the No. 1 ranking.The 28-year-old two-time defe.
articles.body: NEW YORK CITY: Aryna Sabalenka arrived at Flushing Meadows chasing history. She could leave it without the No. 1 ranking.The 28-year-old two-time defending champion is chasing history, aiming to become the first woman since Serena Williams (2012-14) to win three straight US Open titles. But her dip in form has left her hold on the No. 1 ranking looking increasingly fragile. Sabalenka, who made the final of the Australian Open in January and won back-to-back WTA 1000 titles in Indian Wells and Miami has made just one semifinal in her last seven tournaments. The powerful Belarusian, whose recent meltdowns have left spectators gasping, is 17-7 since April.The top seed is closing in on a significant milestone -- 100 consecutive weeks at No. 1 -- but would need to win a third straight US Open title to get there. Sabalenka will reach 99 weeks atop the rankings by the end of the tournament, but with the 2,000 points from last year's title coming off her tally and three players in position to overtake her, extending her reign for another week is no longer entirely in her hands.Elena Rybakina, who clinched the title at Melbourne Park to give her season a rousing start, is less than 500 points behind Sabalenka in the WTA rankings. But the 27-year-old Kazakh’s run into the year’s final Grand Slam has been hampered by a left-ankle injury. Still, the second-seeded Rybakina could rise to No. 1 without playing a match at the US Open, provided Sabalenka, Jessica Pegula and Coco Gauff do not win the title. Should Rybakina reach the semifinals, however, the top ranking is hers regardless of the other results.Sabalenka will bring a little New York spunk to court, kitted out in a basketball-inspired mesh dress with white seams over a bright orange sports bra and matching shorts. Her jewellery -- necklace, bracelet and drop earrings carrying more than 127 carats of coloured gemstones -- channels the city's bold, multicultural spirit. Whether that swagger carries over to her tennis, however, remains the bigger question, as the top seed begins her title defence on Monday against Camila Osorio.At her pre-tournament media briefing, when Sabalenka was asked about her recent run in tournaments, that has left much of the fandom wondering, what’s wrong with Aryna, the world No.1, replied with a smile, “maybe there's something wrong with people.”When tapped about her confidence levels she replied, always confident, before expanding. “That's the beauty of sport, throw tough challenges at me and I will come back only stronger,” she said.There were warning signs in Paris of the world No.1’s struggles. At Roland Garros, Sabalenka was within touching distance of the semifinals, leading Russia's Diana Shnaider 6-3, 5-3, when her game suddenly deserted her. She dropped the final 10 games to lose 6-3, 5-7, 0-6, a collapse as startling as it was troubling.“It wasn't the best period. I don't want to defend myself, but obviously I just don't want to talk about that period,” she said of the last four months. “I've been dealing with several things, but who cares, right? Yeah, I didn't perform my best.”“These tough lessons are definitely going to make me stronger and work even harder,” she finished.The top seed’s outfit may scream New York, but the message from Sabalenka's season is quieter, nothing can be taken for granted. The defending champion may have history in sight, but not everything is in her hands, courtesy of leads she has squandered. In Flushing Meadows, she will need more than her trademark power. It is never about one week or one tournament, it is about finding a way to stay standing when the pressure starts to bite, and carrying that resilience into the homestretch of the 2026 season.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: 8 Semi-Finals, 11 Slams, No 25th Yet: Can Novak Djokovic finally end his Grand Slam drought at US Open 2026?
articles.summary: Tennis News: Three years after winning his historic 24th Grand Slam title, Novak Djokovic returns to New York still chasing the elusive 25th. At 39, the Serbian le.
articles.body: Three years after winning his historic 24th Grand Slam title, Novak Djokovic returns to New York still chasing the elusive 25th. At 39, the Serbian legend remains capable of competing with the best — but with time running out, can the stars finally align at Flushing Meadows?The last time Djokovic stood on Arthur Ashe Stadium for a Grand Slam final, he was making history.On September 10, 2023, Djokovic defeated Daniil Medvedev to win the US Open and claim his 24th Grand Slam singles title, drawing level with Margaret Court's all-time record.Almost three years later, that number remains unchanged.The 2026 US Open, therefore, is about more than another major. It is another attempt to break a record that has stubbornly remained just out of reach.Yet calling the period since his 2023 triumph a slump would be misleading.Djokovic has continued to reach the latter stages of Grand Slams with remarkable consistency. He has reached the semi-finals or better in eight of the last 11 majors, including two finals.What he has been unable to do is win one.Djokovic keeps getting close — but No. 25 remains elusiveThe Serbian's Grand Slam record since his 2023 US Open triumph tells the story.The numbers underline an intriguing contradiction.Djokovic has been a semi-finalist or better in eight of 11 Slams but has failed to add a single title to his collection. His two final appearances came at Wimbledon in 2024 and the Australian Open in 2026, while his latest deep run ended in the Wimbledon 2026 semi-finals against Jannik Sinner.This is not a case of a 39-year-old suddenly becoming incapable of competing with the best.Rather, Djokovic has remained good enough to get within touching distance of another major — but not quite good enough to take the final step. And that distinction could be crucial in New York.The longest wait for a Slam since his first title?If Djokovic fails again at the 2026 US Open, his wait for a Grand Slam title will stretch to 12 consecutive majors.That would be extraordinary for a player who has dominated men's tennis for so long.After winning his first major at the 2008 Australian Open, Djokovic endured an 11-Slam wait before claiming his second at the 2011 Australian Open. He was 23 when he finally ended that drought.A later slump saw him go eight Slams without a title before he ended that wait by winning Wimbledon in 2018.From his 13th major, however, Djokovic needed only six years to reach 24.That makes his current drought historically significant.For the first time since the early years of his career, Djokovic is facing the possibility of going three full years without winning a Grand Slam.The difference now, of course, is age. He was 23 when he ended his first major drought. He is 39 now.Alcaraz and Sinner have changed everythingAge is only part of the explanation for Djokovic's inability to turn deep runs into another title.The bigger factor has been the emergence of Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner.Since Djokovic won his 24th major in New York in 2023, Alcaraz and Sinner have won 10 of the last 11 Grand Slam titles, with Alexander Zverev taking the 2026 French Open.That is perhaps the most telling statistic in Djokovic's pursuit.He has not been pushed out of the elite. He has simply encountered a new generation that has become exceptionally difficult to beat when the stakes are highest.Alcaraz has beaten Djokovic three times in Grand Slam finals, while Sinner has emerged as another major obstacle.Yet Djokovic's head-to-head records show why he cannot simply be written off. He is 5-5 against Alcaraz and trails Sinner only 5-6.That is remarkable for a player approaching 40.The difference is that the younger pair have been more effective at converting their opportunities into Grand Slam trophies.The 2026 US Open could finally give Djokovic an openingThis is what makes the 2026 US Open particularly intriguing.The draw has presented Djokovic with circumstances that have been missing from several of his recent Grand Slam attempts.Most importantly, Sinner is absent after withdrawing with a knee injury.Alcaraz, meanwhile, is returning after a lengthy layoff caused by a wrist injury, leaving questions over whether he can immediately reproduce his best Grand Slam tennis.Djokovic has also avoided 2026 French Open champion Zverev until a potential final.His projected route is difficult but manageable, with a potential quarter-final against Medvedev and Alcaraz among the biggest threats in the latter stages.Compared with recent Slams, Djokovic has one major advantage: one of his two biggest young rivals is absent and the other is returning from injury.The stars, at least on paper, appear to be aligning.But Djokovic's biggest opponent may be timeThere is one factor no draw can remove: age.Djokovic's physical resilience has been one of the defining features of his career. Even at 39, he continues to produce performances that would be extraordinary for almost any other player.His Olympic gold medal in Paris in 2024 was proof that he could still summon his best tennis for a massive occasion.But his overall record since 2023 also reflects the realities of getting older.He won only one title in 2024 and two in 2025, while he remains without a title in 2026 before the US Open. His last ATP Finals appearance also came in 2023, and injuries have increasingly affected his schedule.Preparation has therefore become another question mark.Djokovic does not need to dominate the season anymore. He needs to produce two perfect weeks. At 39, that is considerably harder.Can Djokovic finally win No. 25?The answer is yes — but perhaps never has a Djokovic Grand Slam campaign carried so many qualifications.He is still good enough. The numbers prove it.Eight semi-finals or better in his last 11 Slams demonstrate that he remains capable of navigating the toughest tournaments in tennis. Two of those runs ended in finals.But he is no longer the overwhelming favourite he once was.Alcaraz and Sinner have won 10 of the last 11 majors. Djokovic has repeatedly been stopped at the final hurdle or just before it. And at 39, every Grand Slam represents a diminishing opportunity to add to a record that already borders on untouchable.The 2026 US Open, however, may be different. Sinner is absent. Alcaraz is returning from injury. Zverev is in the other half.Djokovic has four US Open titles and 10 finals in New York, giving him a level of experience few in the field can match. Most importantly, he still believes.Three years after his last Grand Slam triumph, Djokovic is back at the scene of his greatest recent triumph with the same target: 25.The question is no longer whether he can reach the latter stages. He has answered that repeatedly.The question is whether he can win the two matches that have eluded him for almost three years — and finally turn 24 into 25.At 39, it could be his last great chance. And that could make the 2026 US Open the most compelling chapter yet in Djokovic's extraordinary pursuit of history.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Tearful Roger Federer inducted into Tennis Hall of Fame
articles.summary: ‘I’m still writing my love letter to tennis,’ Swiss legend says as he is applauded by former tennis rivals and friends.
articles.body:
An emotional Roger Federer says he is still writing his love letter to the sport that “meant the world” to him as the 20-time Grand Slam champion was inducted into the International Tennis Hall of Fame in Newport, Rhode Island.

Federer, who was inducted alongside broadcaster and journalist Mary Carillo on Saturday, reflected on his storied career in a speech that brought him to tears a few times.

“This is one of the greatest honours of my life,” said Federer. “They call this the Hall of Fame, but fame was never the goal.

“My goal was to spend my life doing something I love … with people who love it as much as I do.”

The Swiss captured a men’s-record eight Wimbledon titles and spent 310 weeks as the world number one. He also won six Australian Open crowns, five US Open titles and one French Open title.

“Tennis meant the world to me. Not just playing, not just winning, but creating something new,” said Federer, who retired in 2022 with 103 ATP Tour titles.

“It’s a mentality I have. I used to play serve and volley, I had a transition game, I played way beyond the baseline sometimes, or on top of the baseline. And I would even try to sneak up on my opponents on my return, and some call it the SABR [Sneak Attack by Roger] today.

“This is what was important to me on the court, but so much of what was really important happened off the court.”

The 45-year-old got emotional while thanking his coaches, doctors and family, including wife Mirka, who praised Federer for his character off the court as a husband, father and friend.

As his name entered the Hall of Fame, Federer said he was proud that Switzerland was coming with him, recalling how he loved watching tennis as a 13-year-old ball boy in Basel.

“I’m still writing my love letter to tennis, and my time as a player is done, but tennis will always stand at the intersection of everything I care most about,” he said.

“My family, our friendships, the past 40 years, the future we’re building — tennis, for me, is responsible for it all. So this is not a goodbye.”

The Swiss said he was “incredibly lucky” to have played with different generations of tennis players, from Andre Agassi and Lleyton Hewitt to Andy Roddick, Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic.

But he added that his induction was not only an opportunity to look back on his career, but also ahead to the future of the game.

“We all leave the court eventually, but the sport keeps evolving,” said Federer. “And as the pace of professional tennis speeds up, as the sport becomes even more global, I so hope it will keep some of that amateur spirit. Keep the camaraderie among the players.

“I hope the players will stay young at heart and stay true to their authentic selves, and always remember, never stop asking questions or taking risks.

“Do things with the game we’ve never seen before. Keep pushing this sport we love to the next level and keep getting better, better, and better.”

Longtime rival and friend Djokovic was among the tennis giants who congratulated Federer on his milestone, calling him a “great ambassador for our sport”.

“We all knew this day is going to come sooner or later, and I don’t think anybody deserves this more than you,” the Serbian said in a video message.

“What you have achieved, what you have represented and still represent for the sport of tennis and sport in general is something truly incredible and remarkable.”

Earlier this week, Federer returned to the US Open for a prime-time exhibition match against Roddick in an event billed as “An Icon Returns to New York”.

Arthur Ashe Stadium was packed full of fans, many wearing hats with the distinctive “RF” logo that became commonplace in the sport during Federer’s decade and a half of dominance, featuring 20 Grand Slam titles.

“It’s great to be back in New York,” Federer said. “I have incredible memories, obviously, of this court, of the fans here, of the city.”

He reminisced about visiting for the first time to play juniors in 1998 and reaching the final. Three years later, his debut on centre court was a straight-sets loss to Agassi.

Federer, who last competed at the US Open in 2019 and retired in 2022, then teamed up with John McEnroe and faced Roddick and Agassi in a doubles exhibition.

images.caption: Roger Federer, in Newport, Rhode Island, US, August 29, 2026, calls himself 'incredibly lucky' to have played with different generations of tennis players [Brian Snyder/Reuters]

articles.title: Roger Federer: Swiss great says Hall of Fame induction 'one of the greatest honours of my life'
articles.summary: Roger Federer says being inducted into the International Tennis Hall of Fame is "one of the greatest honours" of his life.
articles.body:
Roger Federer has been inducted into the International Tennis Hall of Fame, describing the moment as "one of the greatest honours" of his life.

The 20-time Grand Slam singles champion, who retired in 2022, was tearful at the ceremony in Newport, Rhode Island, as he reflected on his glittering career in front of tennis greats including Billie Jean King and John McEnroe.

After making his main tour debut in 1998 at the age of 16, Federer won a record eight men's Wimbledon singles titles, plus six Australian Open crowns, five US Opens and one French Open.

"This is one of the greatest honours of my life," Federer, 45, said.

"They call this the Hall of Fame, but fame was never the goal. My goal was to spend my life doing something I love, with people who love it as much as I do."

Only Spain's Rafael Nadal, with 22 majors, and Serbia's Novak Djokovic, with 24, have won more men's Grand Slam singles titles than Federer.

He won his first Grand Slam title at Wimbledon in 2003 and spent 310 weeks as the world number one - a record until it was surpassed by Djokovic.

Federer also won Olympic doubles gold for Switzerland with Stan Wawrinka at Beijing 2008 and singles silver at London 2012.

He was part of the Swiss team that won the Davis Cup for the first time in 2014.

Federer, who started out as a 13-year-old ball boy at an ATP tournament in Basel, reflected on the lesser-known statistics from his career during his speech.

"I'm talking about the numbers that really paint a picture. Between 1998 and when I first went on the ATP Tour, and when I retired in 2022, I wore more than 5,000 headbands," said Federer.

"That's more than [Bjorn] Borg and [John] McEnroe combined.

"And if you think that's impressive, I wore probably over 7,000 pairs of socks. That's probably twice as many as most of my opponents, because I doubled them up.

"But really, there's no way to measure what it means to be here. It's hard to put it into words."

Federer wiped away tears as he thanked his wife Mirka, tennis idol Stefan Edberg and "every ball kid who ever stood through" his matches.

Federer also said he was "incredibly lucky" to have played with different generations of tennis players, from Andre Agassi and Lleyton Hewitt to Andy Roddick, Nadal and Djokovic.

"I need tissues and sunglasses and everything to protect me right now. This is such a mess," Federer joked.

"As you can tell, I'm still writing my love letter to tennis. My time as a player is done, but tennis will always stand at the intersection of everything I care most about: my family, our friendships, the past 40 years, the future we're building.

"Tennis for me is responsible for it all."

articles.summary: Rachel Stuhlmann has returned to the US Open alongside Genie Bouchard, bringing her strategic tennis storytelling to the sport's biggest stage.
articles.body: It's the final Sunday of August, and we're getting things started this week with a Sceencaps favorite, Rachel Stuhlmann. She's a former tennis player turned influencer who OutKick dubbed the world's No. 1 tennis influencer. It's a title she didn’t take lightly when it was first handed out a few years back. She went all in on doing her part to grow the game of tennis through social media content, and I'm happy to report she's still at it. Rachel, who now considers herself to be the "World’s 1st Tennis Influencer," is back at the U.S. Open churning out content. She's on the court. She's at the parties. And she's even teaming up with retired tennis player Genie Bouchard. Wherever tennis needs her is where you'll find Rachel Stuhlmann. She isn’t just handing out tips on a random court far away from the action. She's on the ground at events and that's intentional. BZZR 'CUTTING OUT THE NOISE' FROM SPORTS SOCIAL MEDIA SPACE GREAT FOR CREATORS, SPORTSCASTER JON ALBA SAYS "I've been creating tennis content for nearly a decade, long before sports creators became as common as they are today. I think that's where the "OG" nickname comes from. I've been fortunate to help pioneer this space and watch it grow," she told the Daily Star earlier this summer. "The way I stay ahead is by continuing to evolve. I don't just post content for the sake of posting - I think strategically about storytelling, what fans actually want to see, and how I can bring them closer to the sport." PAIGE SPIRANAC BACK ON THE GOLF COURSE WORKING ON HER SWING, ELIZABETH HURLEY IN A BIRTHDAY BIKINI & MORE MEAT Rachel added, "Because I work across so many areas of professional tennis, whether it's hosting, media, partnerships, or content strategy, I have access to stories and experiences that most fans don't get to see. That's what I try to share." The strategic storytelling is some of the best strategic storytelling you're going to find, especially when it comes to the sport of tennis. Cheeseburgers Again and More - Gen X Warren M in Florida writes: Hey SeanJo, First day of FBS college football, and I don’t care if it’s Week 0, it’s BACK! We’ve had the games on all day since I got home from a looooonnnngggg bike ride (half Ironman training). Wife has been enjoying watching football with me the past 13+ years, even if my Dolphins have been good to average to awful for a long time. At least her Lions look good. She wants to go to an FAU Owls game, but ever since Lane Kiffin rehabbed his career and bolted for the SEC, they’ve been bad. Originally, I was going to grill up some ribeyes tonight, but something more simple made more sense for college football’s return. I was all about hot dogs, but decided cheeseburgers were more appropriate. Potato salad from Publix plus some Doritos on the side, and a Miller 64 (I burned a lot of calories). The Tecovas beer coozie was free after buying my wife two pairs of cowboy boots in the past year from the local store 😂 They also give free beer, hard seltzers, and whiskey at their stores. When my wife was in love with a pair of boots she tried on, they handed me a double shot of whiskey and soon after, I handed them my card 🤣 👢 Happy wife, happy life! I think we’ll do ribeyes next weekend and make sure I send a photo. Take care! SeanJo I'm right there with you when it comes to Week 0, Gen X Warren. At some point after the UNC win over TCU, I had the multiview going. It was football, football, and football until the second game of the Yankees-Red Sox doubleheader came on. The multiview was still going, but the Yankees game took up one of the boxes. As did a race for some of the time. It was good to have a Saturday with college football on. Week 0 is the promise of things to come and once we get rolling it's full steam ahead. As for the cheeseburgers, I believe you know where I stand on them. I'm a "there's never a bad time for a cheeseburger" guy. ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW! The breastfeeding of her 2-month-old infant while being too intoxicated to care for the child and a 2-year-old toddler played a role in the arrest. The Largo Police in Clearwater, Florida were called to an Extended Stay America hotel last week after a witness alleged Tamisha Brodie, 32, "had fallen while holding her baby and became unresponsive multiple times. The affidavit states that she showed signs of severe intoxication. She had slurred speech, glossy eyes and a strong odor of alcohol. Investigators found empty containers in her room. The kids reportedly had full diapers. There was also no formula for the baby found. Mom was taken to Largo Medical Center for evaluation. Deputies said she had a blood-alcohol content of .295. The infant, who she had allegedly been breastfeeding while intoxicated, was taken to a children's hospital. articles.title: Ignacio Buse coloca a Perú en el mapa del tenis
articles.standfirst: El nuevo número 30 del ranking gana el título en Winston-Salem y ya es el segundo tenista peruano con más títulos de la historia
articles.summary: El nuevo número 30 del ranking gana su segundo título en Winston-Salem y ya es el segundo tenista peruano con más títulos de la historia
articles.body: Perú ya tiene nuevo ídolo local. Ignacio Buse, de 22 años, se ha coronado con su segundo título ATP. Lo hizo en la ciudad de Carolina del Norte, Winston-Salem, por 6-3 y 6-2 ante otra de las revelaciones de la temporada, el británico Arthur Fery. El de Lima, con dos coronas en su haber (Hamburgo y Winston-Salem), ya es el segundo tenista con más títulos en la historia de su país. Solo es superado por el exjugador Jaime Yzaga, que fue capaz de levantar ocho trofeos. Además, Buse está de estreno. Tras su victoria, ha subido hasta el puesto número 30 en el ranking ATP, la posición más alta de su corta carrera. Esto vuelve a situar a Perú en el mapa del tenis. En ocho meses ha pasado de luchar por mantenerse en el top100 a ser una de las 30 raquetas más codiciadas del mundo. En el ATP 500 de Río, con tan solo dos meses como profesional a sus espaldas, ya presentaba indicios de algo más que una promesa. Fue capaza de derrotar al ídolo brasileño, Joao Fonseca, en una tremenda batalla a tres sets en la pista Guga Kuerten, que hace referencia a la leyenda tenística del país. En cuartos volvió a repetir la hazaña con Matteo Berrettini. En aquel torneo, solo le supo parar un muy inspirado Alejandro Tabilo en semifinales. Pero solo tres meses después, levantó su primer título en Hamburgo dejando por el camino a Flavio Cobolli, Jakub Mensik, Ugo Humbert y a Tommy Paul en la final. Como todo ídolo de un país, nunca está solo en la pista. El peruano disfrutó de una grada repleta de aficionados que le llevaron hasta su segundo título en su primer año en el circuito. "Es bastante especial, la hinchada peruana es increíble”, subrayó Buse en la ceremonia de entrega de trofeos.
